title: Not All Prediction Targets Keep Training-Free Diffusion Guidance on the Manifold

paper.title:
Not All Prediction Targets Keep Training-Free
Diffusion Guidance on the Manifold
paper.abstract:
Abstract Training-free guidance (TFG) steers a pretrained diffusion model toward a desired attribute at inference. To be effective, this guidance must be applied from the earliest, high-noise steps of sampling. Because its objective (a classifier or energy) is defined on clean images, ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction models must first estimate the clean image x ^ \hat{x} from the noisy state at each step, and the accuracy of that estimate determines how easily guidance drifts off the data manifold. x x -prediction, a recent alternative, outputs the clean image directly, removing this source of error even at high noise. This is our motivation.
We provide a theoretical analysis of how each prediction target shapes this accuracy, and introduce guided-class FID (Child FID), a metric that exposes the manifold damage standard evaluation misses. Experiments on a new fine-grained bird benchmark and on style transfer confirm that x x -prediction keeps guided samples on the manifold most reliably, making it the strongest foundation for training-free guidance. Code is available at https://github.com/ManLuML/on-manifold-tfg .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Training-free guidance (TFG) [ 7 , 55 , 61 ] steers diffusion models [ 21 , 49 ] toward desired properties without retraining, but strong guidance can push samples off the data manifold. The resulting catastrophic failures (collapsed, distorted images) are qualitatively different from a graceful failure , in which guidance misses the target class but the image remains a realistic sample from the learned distribution. A model whose worst case is graceful failure is fundamentally more dependable: even when guidance errs, the basic contract of generative modeling, producing plausible images, is preserved. Yet this distinction has gone unnoticed. Standard Validity (top-1 accuracy) rewards any sample the classifier accepts, whether on- or off-manifold, a blind spot shared by 15 of 17 recent TFG papers [ 52 ] (Appendix 0.D ). When prior work maximises Validity under strong guidance [ 61 ] , it unknowingly selects off-manifold images fooling classifiers (akin to adversarial perturbations [ 57 , 39 ] ) rather than diverse samples of the target class. The evaluation does not merely fail to detect manifold departure; it actively encourages it. We trace the difference between catastrophic and graceful failure to a design decision predating any guidance algorithm: the prediction target. Three targets have been proposed: ϵ \epsilon -prediction (noise) [ 41 ] , v v -prediction (velocity) [ 35 , 5 ] , and x x -prediction (clean data) [ 30 ] . Guidance operates on the clean-image estimate x ^ \hat{x} : ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction must recover it from the noisy state, whereas x x -prediction outputs it directly. Under identical architecture and training, the three targets produce comparable generation quality, yet differ fundamentally in manifold preservation [ 30 ] : x x -prediction succeeds where ϵ \epsilon -prediction fails catastrophically. Because TFG computes its guidance gradient through this estimate ( ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) \nabla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) ), the fidelity of x ^ \hat{x} directly controls guidance quality. We ask: does the prediction target’s influence on manifold quality, demonstrated at training time [ 30 ] , extend to inference-time guidance? We prove that prediction targets create a strict hierarchy of error amplification ( Proposition 1 ). The mechanism is the recovery formula: ϵ \epsilon -prediction divides by t t , amplifying errors by ( 1 − t ) / t (1{-}t)/t , a factor that diverges at high noise ( t → 0 t\to 0 ). In contrast, v v -prediction attenuates errors by a bounded ( 1 − t ) (1{-}t) factor, and x x -prediction introduces no amplification at all. These per-step errors compound across sampling, causing ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s cumulative perturbation to diverge while x x -prediction’s remains bounded ( Proposition 2 ). The gap further widens with ambient dimension [ 26 , 25 ] (Appendix 0.A ). Controlled ablations confirm this hierarchy: in crossed-lines experiments (identical architecture and training, varying only the prediction target across D ∈ { 2 , 8 , 32 , 128 , 512 } D\in\{2,8,32,128,512\} ), x x -prediction maintains high on-manifold rate while ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses ( Fig. 1 , Figs. 3 and 3 ). Figure 2 : Crossed-lines guided generation ( s = 10 s{=}10 , 100 steps). ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses by D = 32 D{=}32 . Full grid in Appendix 0.G . Figure 3 : On-manifold rate vs. ambient dimension ( s = 10 s{=}10 ). x x -prediction holds > > 93% at D = 512 D{=}512 ; v v -prediction degrades to 21.5%; ϵ \epsilon -prediction drops to 0.5%. Data from Tab. 10 . Validating this hierarchy at real scale demands three evaluation advances absent from prior TFG work: (i) a fine-grained benchmark separating guidance and evaluation classifiers, (ii) a manifold-aware metric, and (iii) guidance-strength sweep plots replacing single-point comparisons. We construct a 143-species bird classification benchmark on ImageNet 256 × {\times} 256 and introduce Child FID (C-FID), FID between guided samples and the target species domain, sweeping guidance strength ρ \rho across Pareto frontiers ( Fig. 4 ). We evaluate four pretrained Diffusion Transformers at comparable quality (FID ≈ {\approx} 2) across all three prediction targets [ 41 , 35 , 30 , 5 ] . At matched classifier accuracy ( ≈ \approx 26.6%), C-FID reveals a 5.2-point gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction ( 32.9 vs. 38.1 ), manifold damage invisible to standard evaluation. Qualitative analysis shows ϵ \epsilon -prediction achieving Validity via classifier-friendly patterns rather than diverse samples ( Fig. 7 ). PixelFlow ( v v -prediction, pixel space) isolates prediction target as the decisive variable: its C-FID reverses under strong guidance while JiT’s continues decreasing ( Sec. 5 ). Across controlled ablations and ImageNet-scale experiments alike, x x -prediction yields the most stable behavior among the three targets for inference-time guidance. Among JiT variants (B/L/H), larger models achieve strictly better guidance Pareto frontiers, a guidance scaling effect in which capacity improves both generation quality and guidance responsiveness. These findings establish prediction target selection as a first-order design decision for inference-time control.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: This paper makes three contributions: 1. Theoretical framework. We prove a strict error amplification hierarchy across prediction targets and show these errors compound into divergent trajectory perturbation for ϵ \epsilon -prediction while x x -prediction’s cumulative error remains bounded ( Propositions 1 and 2 ). 2. Manifold-aware evaluation protocol. We introduce (i) a fine-grained bird classification benchmark (143 species, separate guidance and evaluation classifiers), (ii) Child FID (C-FID) to measure within-class realism, and (iii) guidance-strength Pareto sweeps replacing single-point comparisons. 3. Empirical validation. In crossed-lines ablations, x x -prediction maintains > > 93% on-manifold rate while ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses to < < 1%. On ImageNet at matched Validity, C-FID reveals a 5.2-point gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction; PixelFlow’s C-FID reversal confirms prediction target, not operating space, as the decisive factor ( Sec. 5 ).

sections.heading: Prediction Targets in Diffusion Models.
sections.text: DDPM [ 21 ] established ϵ \epsilon -prediction as the default; score-based models [ 56 ] gave an equivalent view via Tweedie’s formula [ 48 , 12 ] . Salimans and Ho [ 51 ] introduced v v -prediction for improved stability. State-of-the-art Diffusion Transformers achieve comparable quality across all three targets: DiT-XL [ 41 ] ( ϵ \epsilon ), SiT-XL [ 35 ] ( v v ), and JiT-G [ 30 ] ( x x ). Prior work observed ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s training-time error amplification [ 26 , 18 ] ; Jin and Wang [ 25 ] independently confirm this from a dimensionality perspective. We extend these training-time observations to inference-time guidance ( Proposition 1 ).

sections.heading: Training-Free Guidance and Off-Manifold Departure.
sections.text: DPS [ 7 ] and LGD [ 55 ] apply gradient-based guidance for inverse and general problems. TFG [ 61 ] unifies prior methods [ 62 , 3 ] via seven hyperparameters controlling mean/variance guidance and recurrence. All methods depend on clean data estimates x ^ \hat{x} : guidance computes ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) \nabla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) , so the fidelity of x ^ \hat{x} determines both guidance quality and sample realism. Strong guidance produces degraded, off-manifold samples akin to adversarial perturbations [ 57 , 39 ] . Theoretically, nonzero score error enables strong guidance to push samples off the data support [ 6 ] , a failure mode confirmed for CFG [ 8 ] and extending to training-free methods. Our analysis ( Sec. 3.2 ) shows that the prediction target determines the accuracy of the manifold-restoring force.

sections.heading: Guidance for Flow Matching and Evaluation.
sections.text: Feng et al . [ 15 ] derive Flow Matching guidance via velocity-field modifications; we adopt TFG’s post-step correction for its unified DDPM–Flow Matching interface. Standard FID and classifier accuracy cannot distinguish on-manifold success from adversarial artifacts [ 52 , 47 ] : a concern borne out across 17 surveyed papers, most lacking manifold-aware metrics (Appendix 0.D ). We address this with guided-class FID (Child FID) and guidance-strength Pareto sweeps (Appendix 0.C ).

sections.heading: Flow Matching Formulation.
sections.text: Following JiT [ 30 ] , we adopt the Flow Matching formulation [ 32 , 33 , 2 ] : z t = t ⋅ x + ( 1 − t ) ⋅ ϵ z_{t}=t\cdot x+(1{-}t)\cdot\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 𝐈 ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) and t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , where t = 1 t{=}1 corresponds to clean data and t = 0 t{=}0 to pure noise.

sections.heading: Prediction Targets.
sections.text: Three prediction targets have been proposed: • ϵ \epsilon -prediction: The network predicts noise ϵ θ ​ ( z t , t ) ≈ ϵ \epsilon_{\theta}(z_{t},t)\approx\epsilon • v v -prediction: The network predicts velocity v θ ​ ( z t , t ) ≈ v = x − ϵ v_{\theta}(z_{t},t)\approx v=x-\epsilon • x x -prediction: The network predicts clean data x θ ​ ( z t , t ) ≈ x x_{\theta}(z_{t},t)\approx x Given each prediction, clean data can be recovered as x ^ ( ϵ ) = ( z t − ( 1 − t ) ​ ϵ θ ) / t \hat{x}^{(\epsilon)}=(z_{t}-(1{-}t)\epsilon_{\theta})/t , x ^ ( v ) = z t + ( 1 − t ) ​ v θ \hat{x}^{(v)}=z_{t}+(1{-}t)v_{\theta} , and x ^ ( x ) = x θ \hat{x}^{(x)}=x_{\theta} directly. Each formula estimates the posterior mean 𝔼 ⁡ [ x ∣ z t ] \mathbb{E}[x\mid z_{t}] , the flow matching analogue of Tweedie’s formula [ 12 ] , but through parameterizations with fundamentally different numerical stability (Appendix 0.A ).

sections.heading: 3.2 Error Propagation in Clean Data Estimation
sections.text: We analyze how prediction errors propagate to clean data estimates, the quantity that determines whether guided trajectories remain on the data manifold. Proposition 1 (Error Amplification) Let δ ϵ = ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ‖ 2 \delta_{\epsilon}=\left\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}\right\|_{2} , δ v = ‖ v − v θ ‖ 2 \delta_{v}=\left\|v-v_{\theta}\right\|_{2} , and δ x = ‖ x − x θ ‖ 2 \delta_{x}=\left\|x-x_{\theta}\right\|_{2} be prediction errors for each target. The error in recovered clean data is: ‖ x ^ ( ϵ ) − x ‖ 2 \displaystyle\left\|\hat{x}^{(\epsilon)}-x\right\|_{2} = 1 − t t ​ δ ϵ \displaystyle=\frac{1-t}{t}\delta_{\epsilon} (1) ‖ x ^ ( v ) − x ‖ 2 \displaystyle\left\|\hat{x}^{(v)}-x\right\|_{2} = ( 1 − t ) ​ δ v \displaystyle=(1-t)\delta_{v} (2) ‖ x ^ ( x ) − x ‖ 2 \displaystyle\left\|\hat{x}^{(x)}-x\right\|_{2} = δ x \displaystyle=\delta_{x} (3) Proof (Proof sketch) By direct substitution of recovery formulas into the forward process. For ϵ \epsilon -prediction: x ^ ( ϵ ) = x + 1 − t t ​ ( ϵ − ϵ θ ) \hat{x}^{(\epsilon)}=x+\frac{1-t}{t}(\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}) . For v v - and x x -prediction: analogous. Full proof in Appendix 0.B . As t → 0 t\to 0 , ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s amplification diverges while v v - and x x -prediction remain bounded: a strict hierarchy in how prediction errors propagate to clean-data estimates.

sections.heading: Cumulative Trajectory Divergence.
sections.text: Proposition 1 bounds the error at a single timestep, but guided sampling involves many steps; whether trajectories stay on the data manifold depends on how these errors accumulate. Guided sampling is iterative: errors at step k k corrupt the state for step k + 1 k{+}1 . Proposition 2 (Cumulative Guidance Error) Under guided Euler sampling with L g L_{g} -Lipschitz guidance, the cumulative perturbation for ϵ \epsilon -prediction contains a − ln ⁡ t 0 -\ln t_{0} term that diverges as t 0 → 0 t_{0}\to 0 , while the bound for x x -prediction remains 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 − t 0 ) \mathcal{O}(1{-}t_{0}) . Full statement and proof in Appendix 0.B . Early high-noise steps contribute disproportionately large errors under ϵ \epsilon -prediction, corrupting the trajectory for all subsequent steps and driving systematic departure from the data manifold. Remark 1 (Manifold Force Interaction) The score ∇ z t ​ log ​ p t ​ ( z t ) \nabla_{z_{t}}\log p_{t}(z_{t}) decomposes into a denoising component and a manifold force [ 42 ] that pulls samples toward the data manifold ℳ \mathcal{M} . This restoring force is weakest near t = 0 t=0 (pure noise) and becomes dominant only as t → 1 t\to 1 (clean data) (Appendix 0.A ). At the start of the reverse process, where this restoring force is weakest, ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / t ) \mathcal{O}(1/t) error amplification ( Proposition 1 ) is simultaneously at its strongest, corrupting the clean data estimate and allowing guidance to overpower the weakened manifold force, driving samples off ℳ \mathcal{M} . For x x -prediction, no such singularity exists, and guidance and manifold forces compose stably. The amplification factors above are dimension-independent, but prior work [ 26 , 18 , 25 ] has shown that prediction errors themselves scale with dimension: δ ϵ ∼ D \delta_{\epsilon}\sim\sqrt{D} while δ x ∼ d \delta_{x}\sim\sqrt{d} with d ≪ D d\ll D . This base-error gap compounds with the amplification hierarchy; see Appendix 0.A for a detailed analysis.

sections.heading: 3.3 Implications for Training-Free Guidance
sections.text: Guidance methods compute gradients ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) \nabla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) where ℰ \mathcal{E} is an energy function. Theorem 3.1 (Gradient Stability) For a Lipschitz energy function ℰ \mathcal{E} with constant L L , the guidance gradient bound scales as 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / t ) \mathcal{O}(1/t) for ϵ \epsilon -prediction, 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) for v v -prediction, and 𝒪 ⁡ ( ‖ 𝐉 x θ ‖ ) \mathcal{O}(\left\|\mathbf{J}_{x_{\theta}}\right\|) for x x -prediction. Full bounds and proof in Appendix 0.B . The gradient bounds mirror the error hierarchy (assuming comparable network Jacobian norms across targets), indicating x x -prediction yields the most stable guidance gradients among the three targets, particularly at early timesteps where global structure is determined.

sections.heading: From Error Amplification to Child FID.
sections.text: The error amplification hierarchy predicts a specific empirical signature. Cumulative trajectory perturbation ( Proposition 2 ) means that samples departing the data manifold during early guided steps cannot re-enter the target class’s natural distribution. We measure this through guided-class FID (Child FID): FID computed between guided samples of class y y and real images of class y y . A model achieving high Validity (classifier accuracy) but high C-FID produces adversarial-like successes: samples that fool the classifier without resembling real class members. The hierarchy predicts that ϵ \epsilon -prediction enters this adversarial regime at lower guidance strengths than v v - or x x -prediction, a prediction we test directly in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: Applying TFG to x x -prediction.
sections.text: Under TFG [ 61 ] , x x -prediction simplifies guidance: x ^ = x θ ​ ( z t , t ) \hat{x}=x_{\theta}(z_{t},t) directly, bypassing the unstable recovery formula. The full algorithm and latent-space details are in Appendix 0.F .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate whether x x -prediction provides a better foundation for training-free guidance compared to ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction. Full experimental protocols and additional studies are in Appendix 0.G .

sections.heading: 4.1 Models
sections.text: We use official pretrained checkpoints spanning three prediction targets and two operating spaces ( Tab. 1 ); model sources, seeds, and the compute budget are in Appendix 0.I . DiT-XL/2 ( ϵ \epsilon ) and SiT-XL/2 ( v v ) share identical architecture, parameters (675M diffusion model + 49M VAE decoder), training data, and latent space, isolating prediction target as the sole variable. JiT-H/16 ( x x , 953M) is our primary x x -prediction model, chosen over the larger JiT-G (2B) for parameter-scale comparability. PixelFlow ( v v , pixel) provides a critical control: against SiT it isolates operating-space effects; against JiT it isolates prediction target within pixel space. ADM-G [ 11 ] (U-Net, ϵ \epsilon -prediction, FID 4.59) is the only available pixel-space ϵ \epsilon -prediction baseline (Appendix 0.E ). JiT model variants (B/L/H/G) are detailed in Appendix 0.E .

sections.heading: Why models differ beyond prediction target.
sections.text: Li and He [ 30 ] showed that, under identical pixel-space transformer training, ϵ \epsilon -prediction achieves FID 372.38 versus 8.62 for x x -prediction, a 43 × \times gap indicating that ϵ \epsilon -prediction depends on latent-space compression to function competitively. Each model in our comparison therefore represents its prediction target’s best achievable configuration; the architecture and space differences are consequences, not confounds, of prediction target choice (Appendix 0.E ). sections.heading: 4.2 Controlled Ablation: Crossed-Lines
sections.text: To isolate prediction target effects from all other confounds, we train identical MLP-based flow matching models on a 2D crossed-lines dataset (two 1D line manifolds, b = a b{=}a and b = − a b{=}{-}a , with perpendicular Gaussian noise) embedded in ambient dimensions D ∈ { 2 , 8 , 32 , 128 , 512 } D\in\{2,8,32,128,512\} via column-orthogonal projection (Appendix 0.G ).

sections.heading: Architecture and training.
sections.text: For each D D , we train three residual MLPs (256 hidden, 5 blocks) differing only in prediction target, with flow matching for 500 epochs and identical hyperparameters; a separate MLP classifier per D D provides the DPS signal (details in Appendix 0.G ).

sections.heading: Guidance and evaluation.
sections.text: We apply DPS with guidance strength s = 10 s{=}10 , using Euler sampling with 100 steps. Each condition generates 10,000 samples. We report on-manifold rate : the fraction of generated samples within perpendicular distance δ \delta of the true 1D manifold, where δ \delta is the 95th percentile of ground truth perpendicular distances (measurement details in Appendix 0.G ). By embedding the same 1D manifold ( d = 1 d{=}1 ) in progressively higher ambient dimensions, this ablation directly tests the dimension-dependent error scaling analyzed in Appendix 0.A . Full experimental details and additional metrics are in Appendix 0.G .

sections.heading: 4.3 Fine-Grained Bird Classification Benchmark
sections.text: We construct a hierarchical fine-grained classification benchmark to evaluate training-free guidance quality at the species level.

sections.heading: Construction.
sections.text: Starting from 30 ImageNet bird classes (e.g., goldfinch , hummingbird , drake ), we identify fine-grained species from a 525-species bird classification dataset [ 43 ] (previously used for fine-grained guidance evaluation by Ye et al . [ 61 ] ) that map to each parent, yielding 143 species nested within 30 parent classes (2–20 species per parent, mean 4.8; dataset details in Appendix 0.G ). This hierarchy naturally separates two levels of conditioning: classifier-free guidance (CFG) [ 22 ] steers toward the parent class using the model’s own class conditioning, while gradient-based guidance (DPS [ 7 ] ) steers each sample toward a specific species via an external fine-grained classifier 1 1 1 Guidance: https://huggingface.co/dennisjooo/Birds-Classifier-EfficientNetB2 ; evaluation: https://huggingface.co/chriamue/bird-species-classifier . We use separate classifiers for guidance and evaluation to avoid circular evaluation [ 52 ] (Appendix 0.C ).

sections.heading: Why fine-grained birds?
sections.text: Bird classes are already part of ImageNet’s label space, so pretrained models can generate them without domain transfer. Species differ in subtle plumage, beak, and eye markings, requiring semantic shifts that make the gap between classifier-fooling artifacts and on-manifold guidance more visible. The hierarchical structure (parent class → \to species) naturally separates the roles of CFG and DPS, enabling controlled guidance-strength sweeps.

sections.heading: Scale.
sections.text: Each condition generates 64 samples per species across all 143 classes (9,152 images), with ρ \rho swept across 5–10 values per model for six models in total.

sections.heading: 4.4 Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Standard evaluation reports Validity and FID at a fixed guidance strength, but neither metric detects manifold departure. Validity rewards any image the classifier labels correctly, including off-manifold artifacts that fool the network. Parent FID (P-FID, against the full ImageNet reference) rises whether guidance degrades images or successfully shifts them toward a sub-class. A survey of 17 method papers reveals that manifold-aware metrics and guidance-strength sweeps remain uncommon: only two report manifold-aware metrics (Appendix 0.D ).

sections.heading: Child FID and guidance sweeps.
sections.text: We propose Child FID (C-FID): FID [ 20 ] between guided samples and the target domain , the bird species dataset (justified in Appendix 0.C ). Rising P-FID paired with falling C-FID signals successful guidance; both rising signals degradation. Rather than single-point comparisons, we sweep ρ \rho and plot Pareto curves (P-FID vs. Validity, P-FID vs. C-FID; Fig. 4 ).

sections.heading: Inference setup.
sections.text: We standardize all models to NFE ≈ \approx 100 using each model’s native sampler: DiT uses 100-step DDPM, SiT and JiT use 50-step Heun, and PixelFlow uses 30-step × \times 4-stage Euler (NFE = = 120). Latent models use the ema VAE decoder. These settings reduce NFE from each model’s published optimum to enable fair comparison; full configurations are in Appendix 0.G ( Tab. 13 ).

sections.heading: Guidance.
sections.text: We apply DPS [ 7 ] , adding ρ ​ ∇ z t ​ log ⁡ p ​ ( y ∣ x ^ ) \rho\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p(y\mid\hat{x}) at each denoising step with x x -space corrections. Latent models (DiT, SiT) require VAE decoder passes at each guidance step for pixel-space gradients; this overhead is absent for pixel-space models (JiT, PixelFlow). Full configuration details are in Appendix 0.G .

sections.heading: 5.1 Crossed-Lines Ablation
sections.text: The crossed-lines toy experiment ( Fig. 1 b, Fig. 3 ) isolates the effect of prediction target in a controlled setting where architecture and training are identical. As ambient dimension increases from D = 2 D{=}2 to D = 512 D{=}512 , the hierarchy predicted by Proposition 1 emerges ( Fig. 3 ): x x -prediction maintains 93.3% on-manifold rate at D = 512 D{=}512 , v v -prediction degrades to 21.5%, and ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses to 0.5%, consistent with D \sqrt{D} error scaling (Appendix 0.A ). Full metrics and the complete visualization grid are in Appendix 0.G ( Tabs. 10 and 11 ).

sections.heading: Validity alone is misleading.
sections.text: All models show increasing Validity with ρ \rho ( Fig. 4(a) ), but the quality cost differs substantially across targets. At matched Validity ( ≈ \approx 26.6%), JiT-H ( ρ = 3 \rho{=}3 , P-FID 6.9) and DiT ( ρ = 0.1 \rho{=}0.1 , P-FID 6.7) appear equivalent. Under stronger guidance, DiT reaches 29.6% Validity but at P-FID 14.2 ( 2.6 × 2.6{\times} its baseline), while JiT maintains low P-FID throughout. Single-point comparisons obscure this divergence.

sections.heading: Child FID reveals manifold fidelity.
sections.text: Fig. 4(b) disambiguates the P-FID trade-off. At matched Validity ( ≈ \approx 26.6%), JiT-H achieves C-FID 32.9 versus DiT’s 38.1 and SiT’s 34.7, a 5.2-point gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction at identical classifier confidence. DiT’s trajectory is revealing: from ρ = 0.1 \rho{=}0.1 to ρ = 0.5 \rho{=}0.5 , Validity gains come with stagnant C-FID and collapsing P-FID, a characteristic signature of adversarial-like guidance predicted by Proposition 1 . Qualitative inspection confirms this pattern: DiT’s guided samples concentrate on a narrow set of visual templates, whereas JiT produces diverse compositions across the same species ( Fig. 7 ).

sections.heading: Mode collapse.
sections.text: We quantify the diversity loss with DINOv2 Precision and Recall [ 37 ] ( Fig. 5 ). Mode collapse corresponds to high Precision with low Recall: a model that produces a narrow but realistic subset covers the target distribution poorly. DiT ( ϵ \epsilon ) follows this pattern, with Precision peaking at 0.24 while Recall stays around 0.49, whereas JiT-H ( x x ) has lower Precision but higher Recall (up to 0.59). This accounts for the high Precision of ϵ \epsilon -prediction: Precision measures only the realism of generated samples, not coverage of the target distribution, and Recall shows that DiT covers less of it. The behavior is consistent with the error amplification hierarchy ( Proposition 1 ): under guidance, ϵ \epsilon -prediction concentrates samples on a narrow set of classifier-activating features and reduces the support that x x -prediction retains. sections.heading: Prediction target vs. operating space.
sections.text: PixelFlow ( v v -prediction, pixel space) provides a critical control for JiT ( x x -prediction, pixel space). Despite sharing the same operating space, PixelFlow exhibits a substantially worse Pareto frontier: its C-FID initially improves from 44.1 ( ρ = 0 \rho{=}0 ) to 36.2 ( ρ = 2 \rho{=}2 ) but then increases to 47.7 at strong guidance ( Fig. 4(b) ), signaling manifold departure. In contrast, JiT-H’s C-FID continues decreasing throughout the sweep, reaching 30.6 at ρ = 8 \rho{=}8 . This indicates that the prediction target, rather than the operating space, is the primary determinant of guidance robustness in this comparison.

sections.heading: Latent space models.
sections.text: DiT and SiT operate in a 32 × \times 32 VAE latent space, requiring decoder passes at each guidance step. SiT ( v v -prediction) dominates DiT ( ϵ \epsilon -prediction), consistent with bounded error attenuation ( Proposition 1 ), but both are dominated by JiT in C-FID. The VAE’s 8 × \times downsampling may further limit fine-grained guidance resolution, though we do not isolate this factor.

sections.heading: Scaling with model capacity.
sections.text: Among JiT variants (B/L/H), larger models achieve strictly better Pareto frontiers: JiT-H reaches C-FID 30.6 versus JiT-B’s 31.3 at comparable P-FID. Increased capacity yields higher-fidelity x ^ \hat{x} estimates and more accurate guidance gradients, a guidance scaling effect.

sections.heading: Connection to theory.
sections.text: The C-FID evidence supports the error amplification hierarchy ( Propositions 1 , 3.1 and 2 ): samples departing ℳ \mathcal{M} at early steps cannot return to realistic distributions, inflating C-FID even when the classifier is fooled. x x -prediction tolerates aggressive guidance with less manifold degradation. The same ordering holds under other gradient-based methods (LGD [ 55 ] , FreeDoM [ 62 ] ) and on a second fine-grained domain, a 34-species butterfly benchmark (Appendix 0.G , Figs. 8 and 9 ): guidance quality follows the prediction target, not the specific method or domain. Additional ablations are in Appendix 0.G .

sections.heading: 5.3 Style Transfer
sections.text: To test whether the prediction target hierarchy extends beyond classification, we apply DPS to style transfer: guiding generation toward a target visual style via CLIP Gram matrix matching [ 16 ] . We use CLIP ViT-B/16 [ 46 ] for guidance and evaluate with Gram Distance (CLIP ViT-B/32; lower = stronger style match) and Content Accuracy (DeiT-Small [ 58 ] top-1 accuracy on the original ImageNet class; higher = better content preservation). Four WikiArt 2 2 2 https://www.wikiart.org/ styles are evaluated across 100 ImageNet classes (400 images per model/ ρ \rho ). Figure 6 : Style transfer: Gram Distance vs. Content Accuracy. Curves trace models as ρ \rho increases (right to left). Open markers = CFG-only baselines. Lower-right is preferred. Fig. 6 presents Gram Distance vs. Content Accuracy Pareto frontiers. All models trade content preservation for style fidelity as ρ \rho increases, but the degradation rate varies considerably across prediction targets. Overall, the differences between models are less pronounced than in fine-grained classification ( Sec. 5.2 ).

sections.heading: ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction collapse under strong style guidance.
sections.text: DiT’s Content Accuracy drops from 89% ( ρ = 0 \rho{=}0 ) to 1.5% ( ρ = 10 \rho{=}10 ), effectively random, while achieving Gram Distance 5.30. The low Gram Distance is meaningless when images no longer depict recognizable content. PixelFlow ( v v -prediction, pixel space) follows a similar pattern: at ρ = 4 \rho{=}4 , it achieves the lowest Gram Distance of any model (5.04) but at only 37% Content Accuracy, where images lose semantic coherence.

sections.heading: x x -prediction preserves content over a wider guidance range.
sections.text: At high Content Accuracy ( > > 80%), JiT-H achieves better Gram Distance than DiT and PixelFlow: at comparable Content Accuracy ( ≈ \approx 80%), JiT-H ( ρ = 10 \rho{=}10 , Gram Distance 5.48) outperforms DiT ( ρ = 0.5 \rho{=}0.5 , Gram Distance 5.62) and PixelFlow ( ρ = 1 \rho{=}1 , Gram Distance 5.56). JiT-H further reaches Content Accuracy 49.5% at ρ = 50 \rho{=}50 (Gram Distance 5.26), matching DiT’s best Gram Distance while retaining meaningful content fidelity.

sections.heading: SiT is competitive at moderate guidance.
sections.text: SiT ( v v -prediction, latent) achieves a competitive Pareto frontier at moderate ρ \rho : Gram Distance 5.49 at Content Accuracy 85.0% ( ρ = 1 \rho{=}1 ). At stronger guidance ( ρ = 4 \rho{=}4 ), SiT already drops to 71% Content Accuracy while JiT-H retains 87%; by ρ = 10 \rho{=}10 , SiT falls to 38% while JiT-H retains 80%. The Pareto frontiers of SiT and JiT overlap in the moderate-guidance regime and diverge at the extremes.

sections.heading: Consistent failure modes across tasks.
sections.text: Although the quantitative gap between models is smaller than in fine-grained classification, the qualitative failure modes are consistent: DiT’s guided samples exhibit mode collapse and loss of background detail, while JiT-H preserves compositional diversity ( Fig. 10 in Appendix 0.G ). This suggests that the error amplification hierarchy ( Proposition 1 ) manifests across guidance tasks, even when the aggregate metrics show smaller differences. The Gram matrix guidance signal captures aggregate texture statistics rather than fine-grained spatial details, which may explain the reduced quantitative separation.

sections.heading: Additional experiments.
sections.text: We also evaluate DPS on two inverse problems (Gaussian deblurring and 4 × \times super-resolution), where x x -prediction again achieves the best perceptual quality (LPIPS) across all models. Full results and discussion are in Appendix 0.G ( Sec. 0.G.9 ).

sections.heading: Off-manifold degradation is visible but not catastrophic for x x -prediction.
sections.text: Under strong guidance, JiT-H ( Fig. 7(c) ) shows visible quality degradation (posterization and reduced fine detail) but maintains diverse poses, varied backgrounds, and recognizable species-specific features. DiT ( Fig. 7(d) ) achieves 29.6% Validity (higher than JiT-H’s 26.0%), yet its samples exhibit pronounced mode collapse: many images share similar poses, framing, and uniform dark backgrounds, particularly visible in Black Swan and Painted Bunting.

sections.heading: Mode concentration as a failure signature.
sections.text: The samples make concrete the mode collapse quantified in Sec. 5.2 ( Fig. 5 ): the low Recall measured there corresponds to the narrow set of poses and backgrounds DiT repeats here. C-FID registers the same effect: DiT’s C-FID (36.7) remains worse than JiT-H’s (30.6) despite higher Validity. The samples show how it appears: DiT’s ϵ \epsilon -prediction reuses a small set of classifier-friendly patterns rather than covering each species’ variation, whereas JiT-H retains diverse poses and compositions.

sections.heading: Practical implication.
sections.text: Low Validity with preserved image quality (JiT-H at strong guidance) is preferable to high Validity with degraded diversity (DiT): a user can retry generation for the correct class, but cannot recover from mode collapse or manifold departure. This asymmetry further motivates C-FID over Validity as the primary evaluation metric for training-free guidance.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Whether training-free guidance fails gracefully (missing the target but producing a realistic image) or catastrophically (collapsing into off-manifold artifacts) depends on the prediction target. The mechanism is the recovery formula: ϵ \epsilon -prediction divides by t t , amplifying errors unboundedly at high noise; v v -prediction incurs bounded amplification; x x -prediction incurs none. On ImageNet, C-FID supports this hierarchy with a 5.2-point gap at matched Validity (manifold damage invisible to standard evaluation), and PixelFlow’s C-FID reversal under strong guidance isolates prediction target as the decisive factor. The hierarchy extends to style transfer, establishing x x -prediction as the target that keeps guidance failures graceful. The fine-grained bird benchmark and C-FID protocol we introduce let any ImageNet-scale diffusion model be immediately tested for manifold-aware guidance quality, and can serve as a practical diagnostic for evaluating new models.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our comparison involves models differing in architecture and operating space beyond prediction target; no single comparison perfectly isolates it, and the conclusion instead rests on the convergence of five independent control experiments (Appendix 0.E ), of which the latent-space DiT vs. SiT pair and the pixel-space PixelFlow vs. JiT pair are the most controlled within each space. The theoretical analysis assumes Lipschitz energy functions and well-trained models. We evaluate gradient-based TFG methods (DPS, LGD, FreeDoM), not the full TFG parameter space, and all experiments use 256 × {\times} 256 resolution; scaling behavior at higher resolutions remains to be tested.

sections.heading: Future Work.
sections.text: Inference-time scaling methods [ 36 , 29 ] , which are search-based and SMC approaches that compound guidance across many candidates, depend critically on x ^ \hat{x} quality; the prediction target hierarchy should govern their sample efficiency. Video and text-to-image generation present higher-dimensional sequential settings where error amplification compounds across frames, and our dimension scaling analysis predicts even larger gaps between prediction targets. Not all prediction targets keep guided samples on the manifold, but x x -prediction does. For practitioners building inference-time control pipelines, it is the robust foundation.

sections.heading: Appendix 0.C Evaluation Metric Justification
sections.text: As discussed in Sec. 4.4 , standard FID and classifier accuracy are insufficient for detecting manifold departure under gradient-based guidance. Here we formalize the underlying circular evaluation problem and justify C-FID as a complementary metric.

sections.heading: The circular evaluation problem.
sections.text: Training-free guidance computes gradients through an off-the-shelf classifier ϕ \phi , while evaluation measures accuracy using a (possibly different) classifier ψ \psi . When ϕ \phi and ψ \psi share similar feature-space biases, artifacts introduced by ϕ \phi ’s gradients may go undetected by ψ \psi , creating a shared vulnerability . Shen et al . [ 52 ] demonstrate that training-free guidance is more susceptible to such adversarial gradients compared to classifier guidance trained on noisy data, exacerbating this risk.

sections.heading: Child FID as a manifold-aware metric.
sections.text: C-FID ( Sec. 4.4 ) is computed between all guided samples (9,152 images pooled across 143 species) and the full bird species dataset [ 43 ] ( ∼ {\sim} 90,000 reference images). This pooled computation ensures sufficient sample size for reliable FID estimation, while the domain-specific reference detects manifold departure invisible to P-FID. Unlike Validity, C-FID captures perceptual quality within the target class: adversarial-like samples that fool the classifier but lack realistic appearance will inflate C-FID even when Validity is high. Combined with guidance-strength Pareto sweeps, this reveals the full quality–guidance trade-off that single-point comparisons obscure. This connection is not merely analogical: Stutz et al . [ 57 ] established that adversarial perturbations push inputs off the data manifold, and Dai et al . [ 9 ] demonstrated that classifier guidance gradients can be directly repurposed to generate adversarial examples.

sections.heading: Why P-FID misleads.
sections.text: FID is a Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits to two feature distributions [ 20 ] ; the choice of reference distribution is what it measures distance to. P-FID uses the full ImageNet marginal as reference, whereas C-FID uses the target sub-class distribution. As gradient-based guidance succeeds, the generated distribution narrows from the broad parent prior toward a single target species, so its distance to the broad ImageNet marginal grows regardless of sample quality: P-FID therefore conflates successful narrowing with genuine manifold drift. Referenced to the target sub-class, C-FID instead falls when narrowing stays on-manifold and rises when it does not, separating the two cases. The Precision and Recall of Appendix 0.H give a complementary view at a different granularity: a local k k -nearest-neighbour estimate at the sample level rather than a Gaussian summary at the distribution level. The two agree on the ordering of prediction targets, which indicates the ordering is a property of the data rather than of a particular estimator. Validity is blind to both: it accepts any sample the classifier labels correctly, including off-manifold artifacts.

sections.heading: Circular evaluation.
sections.text: FreeDoM [ 62 ] uses identical networks (CLIP, BiSeNet) for both guidance energy and evaluation distance. MPGD [ 19 ] uses ArcFace for both guidance and evaluation. At least 4/17 papers have high circular evaluation risk ( Tab. 3 ).

sections.heading: Manifold claims without manifold metrics.
sections.text: MPGD (“Manifold Preserving Guided Diffusion”) and CFG++ (“Manifold-constrained Classifier Free Guidance”) include manifold-related claims in their titles but report zero manifold-aware metrics: no Precision or Recall.

sections.heading: Good practice.
sections.text: PAG [ 1 ] and SAG [ 23 ] set a higher standard: 50,000 FID samples, Precision/Recall, multi-point guidance sweeps, and (for SAG) human evaluation. These practices remain the exception.

sections.heading: 0.E.1 JiT Model Variants
sections.text: JiT [ 30 ] ( Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise ) is a pixel-space flow matching model that directly predicts the clean image x x instead of noise ϵ \epsilon or velocity v v . The architecture uses a Vision Transformer backbone with Bottleneck Patch Embedding, RoPE positional encoding, adaLN-Zero conditioning, and SwiGLU feedforward layers. All variants share the same architecture and differ only in depth and width ( Tab. 5 ). JiT is trained for x x -prediction; in its high-dimensional pixel-space setting, ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction perform far worse under identical training (a > 40 × {>}40\times FID gap, analyzed below).

sections.heading: Scale variants.
sections.text: We evaluate three JiT variants (B/L/H) to study the interaction between model capacity and guidance quality. JiT-G/16 (2B parameters) is included in Tab. 5 for completeness but excluded from guidance experiments: we use JiT-H/16 for parameter-scale comparability with DiT/SiT-XL, and JiT-G’s FID improvement over JiT-H is in any case negligible (1.82 vs. 1.86) at 2 × 2\times the computational cost. sections.heading: 0.E.2 Why the Comparison Is Not Confounded
sections.text: A natural concern is that our comparison of DiT ( ϵ \epsilon -prediction, latent space), SiT ( v v -prediction, latent space), and JiT ( x x -prediction, pixel space) confounds prediction target with operating space and model size. We argue that this “confound” is itself evidence for our thesis.

sections.heading: 0.E.3 Why ϵ \epsilon -Prediction Requires Architectural Support
sections.text: Among publicly available models with official weights, ADM-G [ 11 ] (2021) remains the only pixel-space ϵ \epsilon -prediction baseline for ImageNet 256 × \times 256. Subsequent work universally adopted one of three strategies rather than continuing pure pixel-space ϵ \epsilon -prediction: 1. Latent compression : DiT [ 41 ] and Stable Diffusion [ 49 ] operate in VAE latent space (4,096 dimensions vs. 196,608 pixel dimensions). 2. Cascaded generation : Imagen [ 50 ] and DALL-E 2 generate at low resolution first. 3. Alternative targets : PixelFlow [ 5 ] uses v v -prediction; JiT [ 30 ] uses x x -prediction. This pattern is consistent with the dimension scaling argument ( Remark 4 ): ϵ \epsilon -prediction requires resolving all D D ambient dimensions of the noise, giving base prediction error ‖ δ ϵ ‖ 2 ∼ D \|\delta_{\epsilon}\|_{2}\sim\sqrt{D} .

sections.heading: 0.E.4 Controlled Evidence from JiT
sections.text: The main body ( Sec. 4.1 ) cites the 43 × 43\times FID gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction under identical pixel-space training [ 30 ] . The full three-way ablation (768-dimensional patches, identical architecture) additionally shows v v -prediction at FID 96.53, intermediate between x x (8.62) and ϵ \epsilon (372.38), confirming the hierarchy is fundamental, not architectural. This ablation is also why we do not retrain JiT with ϵ \epsilon - or v v -prediction for a fully controlled single-architecture comparison at ImageNet scale: such variants are non-functional in pixel space, where the > > 40 × \times FID gap makes the generated images unsuitable for any guidance evaluation, a fundamental dimension-dependent failure ( D = 196,608 D{=}196{,}608 ) rather than a tuning issue (consistent with Remark 4 ). In lower-dimensional latent spaces all three targets remain competitive (DiT, SiT), confirming the failure is dimension- rather than architecture-dependent.

sections.heading: 0.E.5 Capacity-Reversed Comparison: JiT-B vs. DiT/SiT
sections.text: A direct test of the capacity confound: JiT-B/16 ( x x -prediction, 131M parameters) achieves its best C-FID of 31.3 (at ρ = 6 \rho{=}6 ), surpassing both DiT-XL/2 ( ϵ \epsilon , 675M, best C-FID 36.7) and SiT-XL/2 ( v v , 675M, best C-FID 34.4). The 5.2 × \times parameter disadvantage rules out model capacity as the explanation for x x -prediction’s superior guidance quality. The same pattern holds across tasks: JiT-B achieves LPIPS 0.214 on Gaussian deblur ( ρ = 16 \rho{=}16 ) versus DiT’s best LPIPS 0.377 ( ρ = 0.25 \rho{=}0.25 ), despite being 5.2 × \times smaller.

sections.heading: 0.E.6 Convergent Evidence and Scope
sections.text: No single comparison is perfectly controlled, but five independent lines converge on the same hierarchy: 1. Crossed-lines ablation (fully controlled, identical architecture; Sec. 5.1 ). 2. DiT vs. SiT (controlled latent pair, ϵ < v \epsilon<v ). 3. JiT-B vs. DiT (capacity-reversed, 131M x x beats 675M ϵ \epsilon ). 4. PixelFlow C-FID reversal (same pixel space as JiT, v < x v<x ; Sec. 5.2 ). 5. Consistent ordering across four tasks (birds, style, deblur, super-resolution; Appendix 0.G ). The conjunction is difficult to explain by any single confound.

sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: Our analysis applies to gradient-based TFG methods, those computing ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) \nabla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) , including DPS [ 7 ] , LGD [ 55 ] , TFG [ 61 ] , FreeDoM [ 62 ] , and Flow Guidance [ 15 ] . Attention-based methods (SAG [ 23 ] , PAG [ 1 ] , NAG [ 4 ] , SEG [ 24 ] ) do not compute gradients through x ^ \hat{x} and are outside the scope of our error amplification hierarchy.

sections.heading: DPS in latent space.
sections.text: For latent diffusion models (DiT, SiT), guidance with pixel-space objectives requires VAE decoding. The guidance gradient becomes: g t = ρ ​ ∇ z t ​ log ⁡ p ⁡ ( y ∣ D ⁡ ( z ^ ) ) g_{t}=\rho\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p(y\mid D(\hat{z})) (32) where D D is the frozen VAE decoder and z ^ \hat{z} is the latent clean estimate. This introduces three sources of overhead compared to pixel-space guidance: 1. Computational overhead: Decoder forward pass required for every guidance step 2. Memory overhead: Decoder gradients must be stored for backpropagation through D D 3. sections.heading: 0.G.1 Factorial Design Rationale
sections.text: Our experiments use a 2 × \times 3 factorial design : three prediction targets ( ϵ \epsilon , v v , x x ) crossed with two operating spaces (pixel, latent). Model selection rationale and confound analysis are in Sec. 4.1 and Appendix 0.E .

sections.heading: Time Convention Handling.
sections.text: Models use different time conventions: • DDPM (ADM-G, DiT): t = 0 t=0 is clean data, t = T t=T (999) is noise • Flow matching (SiT, PixelFlow, JiT): t = 0 t=0 is noise, t = 1 t=1 is clean data Our guidance implementation normalizes all models to flow matching convention internally.

sections.heading: 0.G.2 Bird Species Dataset
sections.text: Our fine-grained bird benchmark ( Sec. 4.3 ) uses the 525 Bird Species dataset [ 43 ] , a CC0 (Public Domain) image classification dataset published on Kaggle and mirrored on HuggingFace.

sections.heading: Curation.
sections.text: The dataset contains approximately 90,000 images across 525 bird species (at least 130 training images per species, plus 5 test and 5 validation images each). Images were collected from internet searches by species name, deduplicated using automated detection, and cropped so that the bird occupies at least 50% of pixels. All images are resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 RGB JPEGs. Each species includes a scientific name.

sections.heading: Prior usage.
sections.text: Ye et al . [ 61 ] used this dataset and the same EfficientNetB2 classifier for the first fine-grained label guidance study (TFG, NeurIPS 2024); we extend their single-model evaluation to a systematic cross-model, multi-strength Pareto analysis.

sections.heading: Our usage.
sections.text: Of the 525 species, 143 map to 30 ImageNet parent classes (2--20 species per parent, mean 4.8). To our knowledge, this hierarchical species-to-ImageNet mapping, which enables two-level conditioning (CFG for parent class, DPS for species) within a single generation pipeline, has not been established in prior work. We use separate classifiers for guidance (EfficientNetB2 3 3 3 https://huggingface.co/dennisjooo/Birds-Classifier-EfficientNetB2 ) and evaluation 4 4 4 https://huggingface.co/chriamue/bird-species-classifier to avoid circular evaluation (Appendix 0.C ). The species-to-ImageNet mapping and evaluation code will be publicly released.

sections.heading: Guidance Setup.
sections.text: We apply DPS [ 7 ] to each model, sweeping guidance strength ρ \rho while keeping the method minimal: no mean guidance ( μ = 0 \mu{=}0 ), no recurrence ( N recur = 1 N_{\text{recur}}{=}1 ), no Monte Carlo smoothing ( σ = 0 \sigma{=}0 ). This isolates the effect of prediction target on gradient quality without confounding by auxiliary hyperparameters.

sections.heading: Task.
sections.text: Fine-grained bird classification on our hierarchical benchmark (143 species, 30 parent classes; see Sec. 4.3 ). CFG steers toward the parent class; DPS guides toward a specific species via an external classifier. We use separate classifiers for guidance and evaluation.

sections.heading: 0.G.5 Guidance Methods Beyond DPS: LGD and FreeDoM
sections.text: Theorem 3.1 applies to the family of gradient-based TFG methods that differentiate through the clean-data estimate x ^ \hat{x} (Appendix 0.E ). To check that the empirical hierarchy is not specific to DPS, we repeat the bird benchmark with two further members of this family, LGD [ 55 ] and FreeDoM [ 62 ] , sweeping guidance strength at the matched NFE ≈ {\approx} 100 used for the main benchmark. Fig. 8 shows that under both methods JiT-H ( x x -prediction) retains the lowest C-FID frontier, with v v - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction above it, the ordering observed under DPS. sections.text: To test whether the prediction-target hierarchy generalizes beyond birds, we build a parallel fine-grained benchmark on butterfly species. sections.heading: 0.G.9 Inverse Problems: Gaussian Deblur and Super-Resolution
sections.text: We additionally evaluate DPS guidance on two inverse problems: Gaussian deblurring (kernel size 61, σ = 3.0 \sigma{=}3.0 ) and 4 × \times bicubic super-resolution, following the protocol of [ 7 ] . For each task, 1,000 ImageNet validation images are generated and metrics (LPIPS [ 63 ] , PSNR, SSIM) are computed on a 100-image subset; DPS guides the denoising process to reconstruct images consistent with the degraded observation.

sections.heading: Baseline performance.
sections.text: The identity baseline (returning the degraded input) gives PSNR 21.78 / LPIPS 0.5364 for deblur, and the bicubic baseline gives PSNR 23.66 / LPIPS 0.3929 for super-resolution. No model beats these PSNR baselines, so we compare prediction targets on perceptual quality (LPIPS).

sections.heading: Crossed-lines setup.
sections.text: We train identical residual MLP models (256 hidden units, 5 ResBlocks with LayerNorm and sinusoidal time conditioning) on a 2D crossed-lines dataset. The ground truth distribution p ⁡ ( x ) p(x) consists of two 1D manifolds in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} : lines b = a b{=}a (class 0) and b = − a b{=}{-}a (class 1). Points are sampled uniformly along each line ( t ∼ Uniform ⁡ [ − 2 , 2 ] t\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[-2,2] ) with additive Gaussian noise σ = 0.1 \sigma{=}0.1 perpendicular to the line, totaling 12,000 points (6,000 per class). Each 2D point x 2 ​ D x_{2\mathrm{D}} is embedded as x D = x 2 ​ D ​ P x_{D}=x_{2\mathrm{D}}\,P , where P ∈ ℝ 2 × D P\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times D} is a fixed column-orthogonal matrix obtained by QR decomposition of a random Gaussian matrix (seed 42). For each D ∈ { 2 , 8 , 32 , 128 , 512 } D\in\{2,8,32,128,512\} , we train three flow matching models ( ϵ \epsilon , v v , x x prediction targets) for 500 epochs with learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} and batch size 256 (seed 42). A separate 3-layer MLP classifier ( 128 × 128 × 128 128\times 128\times 128 , 100 epochs) provides the DPS gradient signal.

sections.heading: 0.G.11 Choice of Guidance Method: DPS
sections.text: Our goal is to characterize the fundamental relationship between prediction targets and gradient-based guidance quality. This is a scientific question (which prediction target produces the most faithful x ^ \hat{x} estimates and, consequently, the most reliable guidance gradients?), not an engineering question of which hyperparameter configuration yields the best practical results. DPS [ 7 ] is the natural choice precisely because it is the most basic form of gradient-based guidance: a single gradient step ρ ​ ∇ z t ​ log ⁡ p ​ ( y ∣ x ^ ) \rho\nabla_{z_{t}}\log p(y\mid\hat{x}) per denoising step, with no auxiliary mechanisms.

sections.heading: Minimal confounding.
sections.text: DPS isolates the prediction target effect through a single free parameter ρ \rho , the guidance strength. The TFG framework [ 61 ] generalizes DPS with mean guidance ( μ \mu ), Monte Carlo smoothing ( σ \sigma ), iteration ( N iter N_{\text{iter}} ), and recurrence ( N recur N_{\text{recur}} ), but each additional mechanism introduces its own interaction with the underlying x ^ \hat{x} estimate. Under full TFG, it becomes unclear whether performance differences arise from the prediction target itself or from how well each target responds to a particular combination of auxiliary corrections. By stripping guidance to its essential form, DPS ensures that observed differences are attributable to the prediction target’s gradient quality.

sections.heading: Consistency with theoretical analysis.
sections.text: Our theoretical framework ( Propositions 1 , 3.1 and 2 ) analyzes the error in x ^ \hat{x} and its propagation through a single guidance gradient per step, exactly the DPS setting. Using full TFG would require extending the analysis to account for iterated gradient corrections, Monte Carlo averaging, and recurrence, which would obscure rather than illuminate the core prediction target effect.

sections.text: The main text evaluates guidance quality through FID-based metrics (P-FID, C-FID) and classifier-based Validity. Here we complement those results with manifold-aware Precision and Recall curves that directly measure fidelity–diversity trade-offs across guidance strengths.

To be effective, this guidance must be applied from the earliest, high-noise steps of sampling. Because its objective (a classifier or energy) is defined on clean images, ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction models must first estimate the clean image x ^ \hat{x} from the noisy state at each step, and the accuracy of that estimate determines how easily guidance drifts off the data manifold. x x -prediction, a recent alternative, outputs the clean image directly, removing this source of error even at high noise. This is our motivation. We provide a theoretical analysis of how each prediction target shapes this accuracy, and introduce guided-class FID (Child FID), a metric that exposes the manifold damage standard evaluation misses. Experiments on a new fine-grained bird benchmark and on style transfer confirm that x x -prediction keeps guided samples on the manifold most reliably, making it the strongest foundation for training-free guidance. (b) Crossed-lines ( D = 512 D{=}512 , top) and ImageNet (bottom): x x -prediction preserves structure; ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses off-manifold with catastrophic artifacts. 1 Introduction Training-free guidance (TFG) [ 7 , 55 , 61 ] steers diffusion models [ 21 , 49 ] toward desired properties without retraining, but strong guidance can push samples off the data manifold. The resulting catastrophic failures (collapsed, distorted images) are qualitatively different from a graceful failure , in which guidance misses the target class but the image remains a realistic sample from the learned distribution. A model whose worst case is graceful failure is fundamentally more dependable: even when guidance errs, the basic contract of generative modeling, producing plausible images, is preserved. Yet this distinction has gone unnoticed. Standard Validity (top-1 accuracy) rewards any sample the classifier accepts, whether on- or off-manifold, a blind spot shared by 15 of 17 recent TFG papers [ 52 ] (Appendix 0.D ). When prior work maximises Validity under strong guidance [ 61 ] , it unknowingly selects off-manifold images fooling classifiers (akin to adversarial perturbations [ 57 , 39 ] ) rather than diverse samples of the target class. The evaluation does not merely fail to detect manifold departure; it actively encourages it. We trace the difference between catastrophic and graceful failure to a design decision predating any guidance algorithm: the prediction target. Three targets have been proposed: ϵ \epsilon -prediction (noise) [ 41 ] , v v -prediction (velocity) [ 35 , 5 ] , and x x -prediction (clean data) [ 30 ] . Guidance operates on the clean-image estimate x ^ \hat{x} : ϵ \epsilon - and v v -prediction must recover it from the noisy state, whereas x x -prediction outputs it directly. Under identical architecture and training, the three targets produce comparable generation quality, yet differ fundamentally in manifold preservation [ 30 ] : x x -prediction succeeds where ϵ \epsilon -prediction fails catastrophically. Because TFG computes its guidance gradient through this estimate ( ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) 
abla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) ), the fidelity of x ^ \hat{x} directly controls guidance quality. We ask: does the prediction target’s influence on manifold quality, demonstrated at training time [ 30 ] , extend to inference-time guidance? We prove that prediction targets create a strict hierarchy of error amplification ( Proposition 1 ). The mechanism is the recovery formula: ϵ \epsilon -prediction divides by t t , amplifying errors by ( 1 − t ) / t (1{-}t)/t , a factor that diverges at high noise ( t → 0 t	o 0 ). In contrast, v v -prediction attenuates errors by a bounded ( 1 − t ) (1{-}t) factor, and x x -prediction introduces no amplification at all. These per-step errors compound across sampling, causing ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s cumulative perturbation to diverge while x x -prediction’s remains bounded ( Proposition 2 ). The gap further widens with ambient dimension [ 26 , 25 ] (Appendix 0.A ). Controlled ablations confirm this hierarchy: in crossed-lines experiments (identical architecture and training, varying only the prediction target across D ∈ { 2 , 8 , 32 , 128 , 512 } D\in\{2,8,32,128,512\} ), x x -prediction maintains high on-manifold rate while ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses ( Fig. 1 , Figs. 3 and 3 ). Validating this hierarchy at real scale demands three evaluation advances absent from prior TFG work: (i) a fine-grained benchmark separating guidance and evaluation classifiers, (ii) a manifold-aware metric, and (iii) guidance-strength sweep plots replacing single-point comparisons. We construct a 143-species bird classification benchmark on ImageNet 256 × {	imes} 256 and introduce Child FID (C-FID), FID between guided samples and the target species domain, sweeping guidance strength ρ ho across Pareto frontiers ( Fig. 4 ). We evaluate four pretrained Diffusion Transformers at comparable quality (FID ≈ {\approx} 2) across all three prediction targets [ 41 , 35 , 30 , 5 ] . At matched classifier accuracy ( ≈ \approx 26.6%), C-FID reveals a 5.2-point gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction ( 32.9 vs. 38.1 ), manifold damage invisible to standard evaluation. Qualitative analysis shows ϵ \epsilon -prediction achieving Validity via classifier-friendly patterns rather than diverse samples ( Fig. 7 ). PixelFlow ( v v -prediction, pixel space) isolates prediction target as the decisive variable: its C-FID reverses under strong guidance while JiT’s continues decreasing ( Sec. 5 ). Across controlled ablations and ImageNet-scale experiments alike, x x -prediction yields the most stable behavior among the three targets for inference-time guidance. Among JiT variants (B/L/H), larger models achieve strictly better guidance Pareto frontiers, a guidance scaling effect in which capacity improves both generation quality and guidance responsiveness. These findings establish prediction target selection as a first-order design decision for inference-time control. Contributions. This paper makes three contributions: 1. Theoretical framework. We prove a strict error amplification hierarchy across prediction targets and show these errors compound into divergent trajectory perturbation for ϵ \epsilon -prediction while x x -prediction’s cumulative error remains bounded ( Propositions 1 and 2 ). 2. Manifold-aware evaluation protocol. We introduce (i) a fine-grained bird classification benchmark (143 species, separate guidance and evaluation classifiers), (ii) Child FID (C-FID) to measure within-class realism, and (iii) guidance-strength Pareto sweeps replacing single-point comparisons. 3. Empirical validation. In crossed-lines ablations, x x -prediction maintains > > 93% on-manifold rate while ϵ \epsilon -prediction collapses to < < 1%. On ImageNet at matched Validity, C-FID reveals a 5.2-point gap between x x - and ϵ \epsilon -prediction; PixelFlow’s C-FID reversal confirms prediction target, not operating space, as the decisive factor ( Sec. 5 ). 2 Related Work Prediction Targets in Diffusion Models. DDPM [ 21 ] established ϵ \epsilon -prediction as the default; score-based models [ 56 ] gave an equivalent view via Tweedie’s formula [ 48 , 12 ] . Salimans and Ho [ 51 ] introduced v v -prediction for improved stability. State-of-the-art Diffusion Transformers achieve comparable quality across all three targets: DiT-XL [ 41 ] ( ϵ \epsilon ), SiT-XL [ 35 ] ( v v ), and JiT-G [ 30 ] ( x x ). Prior work observed ϵ \epsilon -prediction’s training-time error amplification [ 26 , 18 ] ; Jin and Wang [ 25 ] independently confirm this from a dimensionality perspective. We extend these training-time observations to inference-time guidance ( Proposition 1 ). Training-Free Guidance and Off-Manifold Departure. DPS [ 7 ] and LGD [ 55 ] apply gradient-based guidance for inverse and general problems. TFG [ 61 ] unifies prior methods [ 62 , 3 ] via seven hyperparameters controlling mean/variance guidance and recurrence. All methods depend on clean data estimates x ^ \hat{x} : guidance computes ∇ z t ℰ ​ ( x ^ ) 
abla_{z_{t}}\mathcal{E}(\hat{x}) , so the fidelity of x ^ \hat{x} determines both guidance quality and sample realism. Strong guidance produces degraded, off-manifold samples akin to adversarial perturbations [ 57 , 39 ] . Theoretically, nonzero score error enables strong guidance to push samples off the data support [ 6 ] , a failure mode confirmed for CFG [ 8 ] and extending to training-free methods. Our analysis ( Sec. 3.2 ) shows that the prediction target determines the accuracy of the manifold-restoring force. Guidance for Flow Matching and Evaluation. Feng et al . [ 15 ] derive Flow Matching guidance via velocity-field modifications; we adopt TFG’s post-step correction for its unified DDPM–Flow Matching interface. Standard FID and classifier accuracy cannot distinguish on-manifold success from adversarial artifacts [ 52 , 47 ] : a concern borne out across 17 surveyed papers, most lacking manifold-aware metrics (Appendix 0.D ). The mechanism is the recovery formula: ϵ \epsilon -prediction divides by t t , amplifying errors unboundedly at high noise; v v -prediction incurs bounded amplification; x x -prediction incurs none. On ImageNet, C-FID supports this hierarchy with a 5.2-point gap at matched Validity (manifold damage invisible to standard evaluation), and PixelFlow’s C-FID reversal under strong guidance isolates prediction target as the decisive factor. The hierarchy extends to style transfer, establishing x x -prediction as the target that keeps guidance failures graceful. The fine-grained bird benchmark and C-FID protocol we introduce let any ImageNet-scale diffusion model be immediately tested for manifold-aware guidance quality, and can serve as a practical diagnostic for evaluating new models. Limitations. Our comparison involves models differing in architecture and operating space beyond prediction target; no single comparison perfectly isolates it, and the conclusion instead rests on the convergence of five independent control experiments (Appendix 0.E ), of which the latent-space DiT vs. SiT pair and the pixel-space PixelFlow vs. JiT pair are the most controlled within each space. The theoretical analysis assumes Lipschitz energy functions and well-trained models. We evaluate gradient-based TFG methods (DPS, LGD, FreeDoM), not the full TFG parameter space, and all experiments use 256 × {	imes} 256 resolution; scaling behavior at higher resolutions remains to be tested. Future Work. Inference-time scaling methods [ 36 , 29 ] , which are search-based and SMC approaches that compound guidance across many candidates, depend critically on x ^ \hat{x} quality; the prediction target hierarchy should govern their sample efficiency. Video and text-to-image generation present higher-dimensional sequential settings where error amplification compounds across frames, and our dimension scaling analysis predicts even larger gaps between prediction targets. Not all prediction targets keep guided samples on the manifold, but x x -prediction does. For practitioners building inference-time control pipelines, it is the robust foundation.
